questions.title: Effects of common peroneal nerve injury
questions.question: Effects of common peroneal nerve injury include one of the following:

options.A: Foot drop and inversion of the foot
options.B: Foot drop and eversion of the foot
options.C: Dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot
options.D: Dorsiflexion and inversion of the foot
options.E: Loss of sensation on the medial side of the leg

explanations.A: Incorrect. Foot drop is correctly attributed to loss of dorsiflexion, but inversion is not lost in a common peroneal lesion. Inversion is a tibialis posterior action, and tibialis posterior is a tibial nerve muscle in the deep posterior compartment, which the common peroneal nerve does not supply. The eversion muscles, not the invertors, are the ones lost alongside dorsiflexion here.
explanations.B: Correct. The common peroneal nerve divides into the deep peroneal nerve, which supplies the anterior compartment dorsiflexors, and the superficial peroneal nerve, which supplies the lateral compartment evertors. A single common peroneal lesion denervates both compartments at once, so the patient loses dorsiflexion (foot drop) and eversion together, and walks with a high-stepping gait to clear the dropped foot.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dorsiflexion is indeed lost, matching the nerve's actual effect, but the option pairs it with eversion as if eversion were preserved. Eversion is lost too, since the superficial peroneal nerve that performs it is a branch of the same common peroneal trunk. The deficit is a loss of both movements, not dorsiflexion with intact eversion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This option gets both halves backwards: common peroneal palsy causes loss of dorsiflexion, not a paradoxical preservation of it, and loss of eversion, not inversion. The muscles it denervates are extensors and evertors, not flexors and invertors.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Sensory loss from a common peroneal lesion is over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot, the territory of the superficial and deep peroneal nerves' cutaneous branches. The medial side of the leg is saphenous nerve territory, a branch of the femoral nerve that has no relation to the common peroneal nerve at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that a common peroneal nerve lesion abolishes both dorsiflexion and eversion of the foot.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.35

questions.title: Muscle supplied by the superior gluteal nerve
questions.question: The superior gluteal nerve supplies one of the following muscles:

explanations.A: Correct. The superior gluteal nerve leaves the pelvis above piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen and runs between gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, supplying both. These two muscles abduct the hip and, more importantly, stabilise the pelvis in single-leg stance, so their denervation produces a Trendelenburg gait.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Gluteus maximus, the body's largest muscle and the main hip extensor, is supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve, not the superior one. The two gluteal nerves are easily confused because of their similar names, but they leave the pelvis at different points and supply different muscle groups.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Obturator externus is a deep lateral rotator of the hip supplied by the obturator nerve, which reaches it through the obturator canal rather than the greater sciatic foramen. It has no relationship to the superior gluteal nerve's distribution at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inferior gemellus is one of the short external rotators of the hip and is supplied by the nerve to quadratus femoris, a small branch of the sacral plexus distinct from both gluteal nerves. Its position below piriformis puts it outside the superior gluteal nerve's territory.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Biceps femoris is a hamstring in the posterior thigh, supplied by the sciatic nerve, mainly its tibial division for the long head and its common peroneal division for the short head. It lies well below the gluteal region that the superior gluteal nerve serves.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gluteus medius (with gluteus minimus) as the muscle supplied by the superior gluteal nerve.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.24

questions.title: Muscle supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve
questions.question: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies one of the following muscles:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gluteus medius is supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, which runs between gluteus medius and gluteus minimus after leaving the pelvis above piriformis. The inferior gluteal nerve leaves below piriformis and supplies a different muscle entirely.
explanations.B: Correct. The inferior gluteal nerve leaves the pelvis below piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen and supplies gluteus maximus alone. Gluteus maximus is the chief hip extensor, most active in rising from sitting and climbing stairs, and also stabilises the extended knee through its iliotibial tract insertion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Obturator externus is supplied by the obturator nerve, reaching it through the obturator canal from the medial side of the thigh rather than through either gluteal foramen route. It has no connection to the inferior gluteal nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inferior gemellus takes its nerve supply from the nerve to quadratus femoris, a separate small sacral plexus branch that also leaves below piriformis but is distinct from the inferior gluteal nerve itself. The two nerves travel near each other but supply different muscles.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Biceps femoris, part of the hamstring group, is supplied by the sciatic nerve rather than either gluteal nerve. The gluteal nerves supply only the gluteal muscles proper, not the posterior thigh muscles below them.

questions.learning_objective: Identify gluteus maximus as the muscle supplied by the inferior gluteal nerve.

questions.title: Structure damaged by a first-layer sole laceration
questions.question: A 6 year old boy playing barefooted in his backyard steps on a piece of broken glass and suffers a large transverse cut on his sole, at the level of the midfoot. In the emergency room, the examining physician determines the cut is to the depth of the first layer of the plantar muscles. Which of the following structures is most likely damaged in this injury?

options.B: Tendons of the flexor digitorum longus muscle
options.C: Tendon of the peroneus longus muscle

explanations.A: Incorrect. The plantar arterial arch is formed deep in the sole by the lateral plantar artery, lying at the level of the fourth (deepest) layer alongside the interossei. A cut only as deep as the first layer would not reach it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The tendons of flexor digitorum longus pass through the second layer of the sole, together with quadratus plantae and the lumbricals. A first-layer cut stops short of this plane, so these tendons would be spared.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The tendon of peroneus longus crosses the sole in the fourth, deepest layer on its way to the base of the first metatarsal. It lies well below the plane reached by a wound confined to the first layer.
explanations.D: Correct. The first, most superficial layer of the sole holds three muscles: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis and abductor digiti minimi. A transverse cut at the midfoot that reaches only this depth is positioned exactly where abductor hallucis lies, on the medial side of the sole.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superficial peroneal nerve is a leg and dorsum-of-foot nerve, not a structure found within the layers of the sole at all. It has no course through the plantar muscles that a sole laceration could reach.

questions.learning_objective: Place abductor hallucis in the first, most superficial layer of the sole's intrinsic muscles.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.23

questions.title: Muscle affected by lateral plantar nerve damage
questions.question: Damage to the lateral plantar nerve would affect one of the following muscles:

explanations.A: Correct. The lateral plantar nerve, the smaller terminal branch of the tibial nerve, supplies every intrinsic muscle of the sole except the four the medial plantar nerve keeps for itself. Adductor hallucis is one of those lateral plantar muscles, along with quadratus plantae, the interossei and the lateral three lumbricals.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Abductor hallucis is one of the medial plantar nerve's own four muscles, described as the sole's equivalent of the hand's median-nerve thenar muscles. A lateral plantar nerve lesion leaves it untouched.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum brevis is likewise one of the medial plantar nerve's four muscles, not a lateral plantar one. It sits in the first layer of the sole alongside abductor hallucis, both spared by a lateral plantar lesion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Flexor hallucis brevis is the third of the medial plantar nerve's muscles, despite lying in the third, deeper layer of the sole with the lateral-plantar-supplied adductor hallucis right beside it. Layer position does not predict nerve supply here, only the classic four-muscle list does.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The first lumbrical is the fourth and last of the medial plantar nerve's muscles; the other three lumbricals belong to the lateral plantar nerve. A lateral plantar lesion would weaken those other three lumbricals, not the first.

questions.learning_objective: Assign adductor hallucis to the lateral plantar nerve, distinguishing it from the medial plantar nerve's four muscles.

questions.title: Action of popliteus that unlocks the knee
questions.question: Which of the following is the action of popliteus muscle?

explanations.A: Correct. Popliteus rotates the femur laterally on the fixed tibia to start flexion, which is mechanically identical to describing the tibia rotating medially on the femur. Either description names the same unlocking action, freeing the knee from the rigid, fully extended position it locks into.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The locking mechanism at full extension is described as lateral rotation of the tibia on the femur, driven passively by quadriceps femoris, not as a rotation of the femur produced by popliteus at that stage. Popliteus acts at the start of flexion, to unlock, not to lock.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Locking of the fully extended knee is a passive, obligatory rotation happening automatically during the last 15 degrees of extension, produced by the pull of quadriceps femoris rather than by popliteus. Popliteus performs the opposite action, unlocking the joint.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Popliteus acts entirely at the knee joint, rotating the tibia or femur to unlock the joint at the start of flexion. It has no attachment or action at the hip joint.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Extension of the knee is quadriceps femoris' action alone. Popliteus instead assists the hamstrings in initiating flexion, the opposite movement, by first unlocking the extended joint.

questions.learning_objective: Describe popliteus unlocking the extended knee by medially rotating the tibia (or laterally rotating the femur) at the start of flexion.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.41

questions.title: Nerve supplying the dorsiflexors of the ankle
questions.question: Dorsiflexors of the ankle are supplied by….. nerve?

explanations.A: Correct. The deep peroneal nerve supplies every muscle of the anterior compartment of the leg: tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus and peroneus tertius. All four are dorsiflexors of the ankle, so the whole dorsiflexor group shares a single nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior tibial (tibial) nerve supplies the posterior compartment, whose muscles are plantar flexors and invertors, the opposite action to dorsiflexion. It has no role in the movement this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superficial peroneal nerve supplies the lateral compartment evertors, peroneus longus and brevis, not the anterior compartment dorsiflexors. Eversion and dorsiflexion are separate movements carried by separate nerves within the same common peroneal territory.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sciatic is the parent nerve that later divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves; naming it does not specify which of its two divisions actually supplies the dorsiflexors. The deep peroneal branch, not the undivided sciatic trunk, is the precise answer being tested.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Plantar nerves, medial and lateral, are branches of the tibial nerve distributed to the sole of the foot, well distal to the ankle dorsiflexors. They play no part in ankle dorsiflexion.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute all four anterior-compartment dorsiflexors of the ankle to the deep peroneal nerve.

questions.title: Axillary artery — parts and course
questions.question: Axillary artery:

options.A: Becomes brachial artery at lower border of teres minor
options.B: Axillary vein lies laterally to the artery
options.C: Is divided into three parts by pectoralis minor
options.D: Second part is clasped by the two heads of median nerve
options.E: Gives off the superior thoracic artery from its second part

explanations.A: Incorrect. The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major, not teres minor. Teres minor is a rotator-cuff muscle on the posterior scapula with no relation to this arterial landmark.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The axillary vein lies medial to the artery throughout their course, not lateral to it. This medial position is what keeps the vein out of the way of the cords of the plexus, which cluster around the artery's second part.
explanations.C: Correct. Pectoralis minor crosses in front of the axillary artery and divides it into three parts by its relation to the muscle: the first part lies above pectoralis minor, the second part lies behind it, and the third part lies below it. Each part gives its own distinct branches.
explanations.D: Incorrect. It is the third part of the axillary artery that is flanked by the two roots of the median nerve, which join in front of it, not the second part. The second part instead lies surrounded by the cords of the brachial plexus, which take their names from their position there.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The superior (highest) thoracic artery is the sole branch of the first part of the axillary artery, arising above pectoralis minor before the vessel even reaches the muscle. It is not a branch of the second part.

questions.learning_objective: State that pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts, each with its own branches.

questions.title: Origin of the cephalic vein
questions.question: The cephalic vein:

options.A: Arises in the region of the anatomical snuffbox
options.B: At the elbow, is deep to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
options.C: Terminates by joining the brachial vein
options.D: Is medial to biceps in the arm

explanations.A: Correct. The cephalic vein begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch of the hand, over the anatomical snuffbox region on the radial side of the wrist. From there it ascends along the lateral (radial) border of the forearm and arm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. At the elbow the cephalic vein lies superficial to, not deep to, the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, since both structures run in the superficial fascia with the vein closer to the skin. Being deep to a cutaneous nerve would be unusual for a superficial vein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The cephalic vein terminates by piercing the clavipectoral fascia in the deltopectoral groove and draining into the axillary vein, not the brachial vein. The brachial veins are the deep venae comitantes accompanying the brachial artery, a separate system the cephalic vein does not join.
explanations.D: Incorrect. In the arm, the cephalic vein runs in the deltopectoral groove on the lateral side of biceps, not medial to it. Its whole course, from wrist to shoulder, stays on the lateral (radial) aspect of the limb, which is exactly what distinguishes it from the medially running basilic vein.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Superficial veins of the limbs, including the cephalic vein, carry valves like other veins that return blood against gravity. The claim of having no valves is not a feature attributed to it.

questions.learning_objective: Trace the cephalic vein's origin to the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, over the anatomical snuffbox.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.29

questions.title: Main arterial supply of triceps
questions.question: Which artery is the main supply of triceps?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brachial artery runs superficially down the front of the arm and gives only a few muscular twigs to biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis directly. Its first and largest branch, not the parent trunk itself, is the vessel that actually supplies triceps.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The dorsal scapular artery contributes to the anastomosis around the scapula on the posterior chest wall, well proximal to the arm. It plays no direct part in supplying triceps.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior circumflex humeral artery winds around the surgical neck of the humerus with the axillary nerve, chiefly supplying deltoid and the shoulder joint. It does not reach down into the posterior compartment of the arm where triceps lies.
explanations.D: Correct. The profunda brachii artery is the first and largest branch of the brachial artery, arising just below teres major and running backward with the radial nerve between the long and medial heads of triceps before winding into the spiral groove. Along this course it is the chief arterial supply of triceps.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The radial artery is a terminal branch of the brachial artery formed only at the elbow, in the forearm, well distal to triceps. It has no role in supplying a muscle located in the arm above it.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the profunda brachii artery as the main arterial supply of triceps.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.29

questions.title: Muscle of the thenar eminence
questions.question: Which of the following muscles is part of thenar eminence?

explanations.A: Correct. The thenar eminence is formed by three muscles, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis, all supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. Flexor pollicis brevis is one of these three, flexing the thumb's metacarpophalangeal joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lumbricals lie deep in the palm proper, arising from the flexor digitorum profundus tendons, and are not part of the superficial thenar bulge at the base of the thumb. They belong to a different functional group entirely, flexing the metacarpophalangeal and extending the interphalangeal joints.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Flexor pollicis longus is a long forearm flexor whose tendon merely passes through the carpal tunnel to reach the thumb; it does not have its belly in the thenar eminence. Only the short (brevis) thumb muscles form the eminence itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adductor pollicis lies deep, in its own adductor compartment rather than within the thenar eminence, and is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve rather than the median nerve. This is a classic distractor, since both muscles sound alike but differ completely in position and nerve supply.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Opponens digiti minimi is a hypothenar, not thenar, muscle, opposing the little finger rather than the thumb. It is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve, on the opposite side of the hand from the thenar group.

questions.learning_objective: Name flexor pollicis brevis as one of the three median-nerve muscles forming the thenar eminence.

questions.title: Nerve injured causing elbow, wrist and finger drop
questions.question: Mohammed is a 14-year-old boy who was horse-riding early today. He was rushed into hospital after falling off his horse. After a thorough examination, it was discovered that he had elbow drop, wrist drop, and finger drop. Which one of the following nerves is injured?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Axillary nerve injury weakens deltoid-driven abduction and flattens the contour of the shoulder; it does not affect the elbow, wrist or finger extensors at all. The described triad of drops points to a nerve supplying extensor muscle groups, not the axillary nerve's territory.
explanations.B: Correct. The radial nerve supplies triceps at the elbow and every extensor of the wrist and fingers in the forearm. Its injury, classically from trauma along its course such as a fall, therefore produces the combined picture of elbow extension weakness, wrist drop and finger drop described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The median nerve is a flexor-side nerve, supplying most forearm flexors and the thenar muscles; its injury weakens flexion and thumb opposition, not extension. It cannot explain a picture built entirely from dropped, unextended joints.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve supplies intrinsic hand muscles and produces a claw-hand deformity from loss of the interossei and medial lumbricals, not the proximal elbow, wrist and finger extensor drop seen here. Its territory does not reach the elbow or wrist extensors at all.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm flexors, biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis, and ends as a purely sensory nerve in the forearm. It has no relationship to any of the three drop signs described.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute a combined elbow, wrist and finger drop to radial nerve injury, since the nerve supplies every extensor group along its course.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.39

questions.title: Structure protecting the brachial artery at venipuncture
questions.question: While taking a blood sample from the median cubital vein. Which one of the following structures protects the brachial artery from being injured?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Brachialis lies deep in the cubital fossa, beneath the brachial artery rather than between the artery and the superficial median cubital vein where the needle passes. It cannot be the structure that shields the artery from a needle entering from the skin surface.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The biceps tendon runs centrally in the cubital fossa on its way to the radial tuberosity, but it is the fibrous sheet that spreads medially from it, not the tendon itself, that overlies the vein-to-artery gap. The tendon and its aponeurotic expansion are related but distinct structures.
explanations.C: Correct. The bicipital aponeurosis is a fibrous expansion from the biceps tendon that spreads medially across the cubital fossa, lying directly beneath the median cubital vein and separating it from the brachial artery and median nerve below. This protective layer is exactly why the median cubital vein is the standard, safer site for venepuncture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The radial nerve lies laterally in the cubital fossa, between brachioradialis and brachialis, well away from the medially placed median cubital vein. It plays no protective role at the site where the vein is punctured.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The median nerve lies medial to the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, but it is one of the structures being protected by the bicipital aponeurosis, not the protective structure itself. Confusing the protected structures with the protecting one is the trap this option sets.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the bicipital aponeurosis as the structure separating the median cubital vein from the brachial artery during venepuncture.

questions.title: A true statement about the brachial artery
questions.question: The brachial artery:

options.A: Crosses anterior to the median nerve in the arm
options.B: Gives off the nutrient artery to the humerus
options.D: Has the ulnar nerve on its medial side

explanations.A: Incorrect. In the arm the median nerve crosses in front of the brachial artery, from its lateral to its medial side, rather than the artery crossing in front of the nerve. Describing the relation the other way around reverses which structure passes over which.
explanations.B: Correct. Among its branch groups, the brachial artery gives a nutrient artery to the shaft of the humerus, alongside the profunda brachii, the superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries, and muscular branches to biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis. This nutrient artery is a small but distinct branch, separate from the larger muscular and collateral vessels the same trunk supplies. Enumerating it correctly is what this straightforward recall item is testing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The brachial artery is superficial throughout the arm, covered only by skin and fascia, not deep to biceps. Its superficial position is exactly what makes it palpable and vulnerable along the medial border of biceps.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve leaves the brachial artery's company in the middle of the arm, piercing the medial intermuscular septum to run posteriorly behind the medial epicondyle, so it is not found on the artery's medial side for the artery's whole course. The median nerve, not the ulnar, stays with the artery down to the cubital fossa.

questions.learning_objective: Include the nutrient artery to the humerus among the brachial artery's branches.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.29

questions.title: Muscles paralysed by an anterior interosseous nerve lesion
questions.question: A patient with a deep stab wound in the middle of the forearm. Examination indicates a lesion of the anterior interosseous nerve. Which of the following muscles is paralyzed?

options.B: Flexor pollicis longus and opponens pollicis
options.C: Flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus

explanations.A: Incorrect. Flexor pollicis brevis is a thenar muscle supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve in the hand, not by the anterior interosseous branch in the forearm. Pairing it with flexor pollicis longus mixes a hand muscle into a purely forearm nerve's territory.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Opponens pollicis is likewise a thenar muscle on the median nerve's recurrent branch, supplied distally in the hand rather than by the anterior interosseous nerve in the forearm. The anterior interosseous nerve is purely motor to forearm muscles, never reaching this far distally.
explanations.C: Correct. The anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve given off just below the elbow, supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus. A lesion paralyses these muscles, producing the classic pinch weakness where the patient cannot form a round 'OK' sign.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum superficialis is supplied directly by the median nerve trunk in the forearm, before the anterior interosseous branch is given off, so it is unaffected by an isolated anterior interosseous lesion. Only the profundus tendons to the index and middle fingers, the ones on the anterior interosseous side, are lost.

questions.learning_objective: List flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus as the muscles lost in anterior interosseous nerve syndrome.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.33

questions.title: Muscles tested by spreading the fingers
questions.question: Part of a physical examination to evaluate muscle function in the hand, a physician holds the four fingers (digits 2 through 5) and asks the patient to spread their fingers. What muscle(s) is are the doctor testing?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints, the writing position of the hand, but they do not abduct the fingers apart from one another. Spreading the fingers is not a lumbrical action.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The palmar interossei perform the opposite movement to the one being tested: they adduct the fingers toward the axis of the middle finger, drawing the spread fingers back together rather than spreading them apart.
explanations.C: Correct. The four dorsal interossei abduct the fingers away from the axis of the middle finger, so asking a patient to spread the fingers apart specifically tests these muscles. All seven interossei, dorsal and palmar together, are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints, a movement unrelated to spreading the fingers apart at the metacarpophalangeal joints. It is tested instead by holding one finger straight and asking the patient to flex the others.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Flexor digitorum profundus flexes the distal interphalangeal joints, again a flexion movement rather than the abduction being examined here. Neither long flexor tendon abducts the fingers.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute finger abduction (spreading the fingers) to the dorsal interossei, supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.27

questions.title: Ligament preventing hip hyperabduction
questions.question: Which one of the following ligaments prevents Hyperabduction of the Hip joint?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The iliofemoral ligament is the Y-shaped, anteriorly placed ligament and the strongest in the body, but its job is to check hyperextension of the hip, not hyperabduction. It winds tight as the hip extends, the movement it limits.
explanations.B: Correct. The pubofemoral ligament runs anteroinferiorly from the pubic part of the acetabulum to the femur, and it is this ligament that limits excessive abduction and extension of the hip. Along with the iliofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments it spirals to tighten in extension, but abduction is its own particular limit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ischiofemoral ligament lies posteriorly and limits internal rotation and adduction of the hip, movements essentially opposite to abduction. It does not restrain hyperabduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The round ligament (ligamentum teres) is an intracapsular structure running from the femoral head to the acetabular notch, carrying a small artery to the head rather than acting as a restraining capsular ligament. It contributes little to joint stability and does not specifically limit abduction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The transverse acetabular ligament bridges the acetabular notch, completing the rim of the acetabulum and converting the notch into a foramen for vessels and the ligamentum teres. It plays a structural role in the socket, not a restraining role at the extremes of hip movement.

questions.learning_objective: Assign hip hyperabduction limitation to the pubofemoral ligament, distinct from the iliofemoral (hyperextension) and ischiofemoral (adduction/internal rotation) ligaments.

field_notes.keySource: printed key positioned at right margin beside question number, p.41

questions.title: Surface landmark of the ulnar artery's origin
questions.question: At which anatomical landmark (surface anatomy) does the ulnar artery originate?

options.B: Opposite the neck of the radius

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lower border of teres major is where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery, a landmark well proximal to where the ulnar artery itself begins. The ulnar artery does not originate until the brachial artery divides much further down, at the elbow.
explanations.B: Correct. The ulnar artery begins in the cubital fossa, below the elbow joint, as the larger of the two terminal branches of the brachial artery, at the level opposite the neck of the radius. This is the same level at which the brachial artery's other terminal branch, the radial artery, also begins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral border of the first rib is the landmark for the axillary artery's own origin, where it continues from the subclavian artery, not for the ulnar artery. The ulnar artery arises much further distally, at the elbow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anatomical snuffbox is on the radial (lateral) side of the wrist, crossed by the radial artery, not the site where the ulnar artery begins. The ulnar artery instead approaches the wrist on the medial side, alongside the ulnar nerve.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The flexor retinaculum lies at the wrist, where the ulnar artery ends by passing superficial to it to form the superficial palmar arch, not where the artery originates. Origin and termination sit at opposite ends of its forearm course.

questions.learning_objective: Place the ulnar artery's origin at the level of the radial neck, in the cubital fossa, as the brachial artery's larger terminal branch.

questions.title: Origin of the suprascapular nerve
questions.question: Suprascapular nerve is branch from ……

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dorsal scapular and long thoracic nerves are the classic examples of branches arising directly from the roots of the brachial plexus, before any trunk has formed. The suprascapular nerve arises one stage later, from the upper trunk.
explanations.B: Correct. The suprascapular nerve arises from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus, carrying C5 and C6 fibres. It runs laterally across the posterior triangle of the neck and passes through the suprascapular notch to supply supraspinatus and infraspinatus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no 'middle trunk' in the brachial plexus; the three trunks are upper, middle and lower, but the suprascapular nerve specifically arises from the upper trunk, not from an intermediate level between it and the lower trunk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lower trunk is formed from the C8 and T1 roots and gives rise to structures feeding the medial cord and ultimately the ulnar nerve territory. The suprascapular nerve's C5, C6 fibres place its origin at the upper trunk instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The posterior cord is a later stage of the plexus, formed from the posterior divisions of all three trunks, giving the axillary and radial nerves among others. The suprascapular nerve branches off much earlier, at the trunk level, before the cords have even formed.

questions.learning_objective: Trace the suprascapular nerve's origin to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.

questions.title: Where the dorsalis pedis artery begins
questions.question: Dorsalis pedis artery begins .. ………

explanations.A: Incorrect. Behind the medial malleolus is where the posterior tibial artery passes on its way into the sole, not where the dorsalis pedis artery begins. Dorsalis pedis is a dorsal, not a posteromedial, vessel.
explanations.B: Correct. The anterior tibial artery becomes the dorsalis pedis artery in front of the ankle, midway between the medial and lateral malleoli, deep to the extensor retinacula. From there it crosses the dorsum of the foot before diving into the sole to complete the deep plantar arch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The flexor retinaculum is a wrist structure of the upper limb; the lower-limb structures analogous to it at the ankle are the extensor and flexor retinacula, and even the ankle's flexor retinaculum lies posteromedially, not at the site where dorsalis pedis begins anteriorly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Behind the lateral malleolus is where the peroneal tendons and the small saphenous vein's territory lie, not the starting point of dorsalis pedis, which begins anteriorly rather than posterolaterally.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The sole is where dorsalis pedis ends, diving between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous to complete the deep plantar arch, not where it begins. Its origin is dorsal, at the front of the ankle, well before it ever reaches the sole.

questions.learning_objective: Locate the dorsalis pedis artery's origin at the front of the ankle, midway between the two malleoli.
